title: Tiny reed snakes cartwheel away from danger, four times faster than they can slither
body: On 19 October 2026 Yosuke Kojima of Toho University in Japan and colleagues reported in Current Biology how dwarf reed snakes of the genus Pseudorabdion, 11 to 28 cm long and found on the forest floor in Southeast Asia, roll like a wheel to escape, as [ScienceDaily](https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261023023718.htm) reported. Snakes normally slither, pushing body waves sideways against the ground; rolling, these reached 1.72 to 3.69 metres a second, about four times their fastest slither. Each stroke starts with the body curled into a C and the head lifted, facing forward; the snake whips its tail out behind, briefly airborne, swings it forward and down past the head, lands it in front, and the next roll begins on the other side. A wheel needs an axle, but the snake has none: the rear of the body does the spinning while the head barely turns and holds an almost constant height, higher and steadier at speed, and on a 2.2 m track the rollers kept inside a strip 20 cm wide. All 13 dwarf reed snakes tested rolled; their cousins of the genus Calamaria never did. Rolling is probably costly, and how long a snake can keep it up is unknown.

slides.question: Rolling like a wheel, a dwarf reed snake reaches up to how many metres per second?
slides.explanation: Up to 3.69 m/s, about 13 km/h, in Toho University’s high-speed videos; the slowest roll measured was 1.72 m/s. That is about four times the snakes’ fastest slither.

slides.alt: Animation on leaf-litter green: a copper snake rolling as a loop with its head held steady, a race between a slithering and a rolling snake over 2.2 m, the stroke drawn step by step from a C shape to a tail landing in front, a dashed head-height line, and panels on the test and the hoop-snake tales.
slides.music: “Goblin Tinker Soldier Spy” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Race a rolling snake against a slithering one over the study’s 2.2 m track. Find a rolling speed that crosses it in under a second.
slides.takeaway: Anything above 2.2 m/s does it; the fastest measured roll, 3.69 m/s, takes 0.6 s, and the slither, at a quarter of the speed, four times as long. Rolling is a sprint, probably costly, and nobody knows how long it lasts.

steps.label: Curl into a C, head up, facing forward
Whip the tail out behind, briefly airborne
Swing it forward and down past the head
Land it in front: next roll, other side

slides.heading: A wheel and a rolling snake

left.label: A wheel
left.text: Spins around an axle: the hub stays still while the rim turns. No animal has evolved one, since no living part can spin freely.

right.label: The snake
right.text: No axle: the rear of the body does the spinning while the head barely turns and holds its height, like a hub without one.

slides.question: How did the dwarf reed snakes keep their heads steady while cartwheeling in the Toho University videos?
options: The rear of the body did the spinning
They used their tails as an axle
slides.explanation: The head rotated far less than the rest of the body and kept a nearly constant height, higher and steadier at speed, with no mechanical separation between the spinning and the steady parts.
